Usage: tar [OPTION...] [FILE]...
GNU 'tar' saves many files together into a single tape or disk archive, and can
restore individual files from the archive.

Examples:
  tar -cf archive.tar foo bar  # Create archive.tar from files foo and bar.
  tar -tvf archive.tar         # List all files in archive.tar verbosely.
  tar -xf archive.tar          # Extract all files from archive.tar.

 Main operation mode:
  -A, --catenate, --concatenate   append tar files to an archive
  -c, --create               create a new archive
      --delete               delete from the archive (not on mag tapes!)
  -d, --diff, --compare      find differences between archive and file system
  -r, --append               append files to the end of an archive
      --test-label           test the archive volume label and exit
  -t, --list                 list the contents of an archive
  -u, --update               only append files newer than copy in archive
  -x, --extract, --get       extract files from an archive

 Operation modifiers:

      --check-device         check device numbers when creating incremental
                             archives (default)
  -g, --listed-incremental=FILE   handle new GNU-format incremental backup
  -G, --incremental          handle old GNU-format incremental backup
      --hole-detection=TYPE  technique to detect holes
      --ignore-failed-read   do not exit with nonzero on unreadable files
      --level=NUMBER         dump level for created listed-incremental archive
      --no-check-device      do not check device numbers when creating
                             incremental archives
      --no-seek              archive is not seekable
  -n, --seek                 archive is seekable
      --occurrence[=NUMBER]  process only the NUMBERth occurrence of each file
                             in the archive; this option is valid only in
                             conjunction with one of the subcommands --delete,
                             --diff, --extract or --list and when a list of
                             files is given either on the command line or via
                             the -T option; NUMBER defaults to 1
      --sparse-version=MAJOR[.MINOR]
                             set version of the sparse format to use (implies
                             --sparse)
  -S, --sparse               handle sparse files efficiently

 Local file name selection:
      --add-file=FILE        add given FILE to the archive (useful if its name
                             starts with a dash)
  -C, --directory=DIR        change to directory DIR
      --exclude=PATTERN      exclude files, given as a PATTERN
      --exclude-backups      exclude backup and lock files
      --exclude-caches       exclude contents of directories containing
                             CACHEDIR.TAG, except for the tag file itself
      --exclude-caches-all   exclude directories containing CACHEDIR.TAG
      --exclude-caches-under exclude everything under directories containing
                             CACHEDIR.TAG
      --exclude-ignore=FILE  read exclude patterns for each directory from
                             FILE, if it exists
      --exclude-ignore-recursive=FILE
                             read exclude patterns for each directory and its
                             subdirectories from FILE, if it exists
      --exclude-tag=FILE     exclude contents of directories containing FILE,
                             except for FILE itself
      --exclude-tag-all=FILE exclude directories containing FILE
      --exclude-tag-under=FILE   exclude everything under directories
                             containing FILE
      --exclude-vcs          exclude version control system directories
      --exclude-vcs-ignores  read exclude patterns from the VCS ignore files
      --no-null              disable the effect of the previous --null option
      --no-recursion         avoid descending automatically in directories
      --no-unquote           do not unquote input file or member names
      --no-verbatim-files-from   -T treats file names starting with dash as
                             options (default)
      --null                 -T reads null-terminated names; implies
                             --verbatim-files-from
      --recursion            recurse into directories (default)
  -T, --files-from=FILE      get names to extract or create from FILE
      --unquote              unquote input file or member names (default)
      --verbatim-files-from  -T reads file names verbatim (no escape or option
                             handling)
  -X, --exclude-from=FILE    exclude patterns listed in FILE

The user asks: "How do I include all resources, even those not using docker compose?" Likely they want to use `--all-resources` flag with `docker compose` commands. The help shows `--all-resources` includes all resources, even those not used by services. So answer: use `--all-resources` flag. Provide example.

We should answer directly.</think>The `docker compose` command has a dedicated option for this:

```bash
docker compose --all-resources <command>
```

`--all-resources` tells Docker Compose to include **all** resources (volumes, networks, etc.) even if they aren’t directly referenced by any service in the compose file.

**Typical usage examples**

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| List **all** volumes (including those not used by any service) | `docker compose --all-resources volumes` |
| List **all** networks (including those not used by any service) | `docker compose --all-resources networks` |
| Show the full config, including unused resources | `docker compose --all-resources config` |
| Start services **and** bring up any associated volumes/networks | `docker compose --all-resources up` |

You can combine `--all-resources` with any other `docker compose` option (e.g., `-f docker-compose.yml`, `-p myproject`, etc.).

NAME
       git-rebase - Reapply commits on top of another base tip

SYNOPSIS
       git rebase [-i | --interactive] [<options>] [--exec <cmd>]

       to reorder or combine commits: see INTERACTIVE MODE below for how to do that.

       For example, imagine that you have been working on the topic branch in this history, and you
       want to "catch up" to the work done on the master branch.

                     A---B---C topic
                    /
               D---E---F---G master

       You want to transplant the commits you made on topic since it diverged from master (i.e. A,
       B, and C), on top of the current master. You can do this by running git rebase master while
       the topic branch is checked out. If you want to rebase topic while on another branch, git
       rebase master topic is a shortcut for git checkout topic && git rebase master.

                            /

       problematic commit and leave conflict markers. If this happens, you can do one of these
       things:

        1. Resolve the conflict. You can use git diff to find the markers (<<<<<<) and make edits
           to resolve the conflict. For each file you edit, you need to tell Git that the conflict
           has been resolved. You can mark the conflict as resolved with git add <filename>. After
           resolving all of the conflicts, you can continue the rebasing process with

               git rebase --continue

        2. Stop the git rebase and return your branch to its original state with

               git rebase --abort

        3. Skip the commit that caused the merge conflict with

               git rebase --skip


**What it does**

- After you have resolved any merge‑conflict markers that appeared during an interactive rebase, running `git rebase --continue` tells Git to finish the current rebase step and move on to the next commit (or, if there are no more commits, to complete the rebase).

**Typical workflow**

1. Start the rebase (e.g., `git rebase -i <base>`).  
2. If a conflict occurs, Git pauses the rebase and lists the files with conflicts.  
3. Edit the files to resolve the conflicts, then stage the resolved files:

   ```bash
   git add <resolved-file>
   ```

   (You can also use `git mergetool` or any other merge‑resolution tool.)

4. Once all conflicts are resolved, run:

   ```bash
   git rebase --continue
   ```

5. Repeat steps 2‑4 for each subsequent commit that needs conflict resolution, or simply `git rebase --continue` if no more conflicts remain.

**Related options**

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `--abort` | Cancel the entire rebase and return the branch to its original state. |
| `--skip`  | Skip the current commit (useful when you don’t want a particular commit). |
| `--quit`  | Finish the rebase without applying any remaining commits (exits after the current step). |

So the concise syntax you need is simply `git rebase --continue`.

```bash
--check-device          # check device numbers when creating incremental archives (default)
--no-check-device       # do NOT check device numbers when creating incremental archives
```

**Typical usage**

```bash
# Create an incremental backup and *check* device numbers (the default behaviour)
tar --create --gzip --check-device --file=backup.tar.gz /path/to/data

# Explicitly enable the check (redundant, but makes the intent clear)
tar -c --check-device -f backup.tar.gz /path/to/data

# Disable the check (useful if you know the device numbers are already correct
# or you want to avoid the warning/error)
tar -c --no-check-device -f backup.tar.gz /path/to/data
```

**What it does**

When an incremental backup is created, `tar` records the device number (major/minor) of each file.  
- With **`--check-device`** (the default), `tar` verifies that the device number of each file matches the one stored in the previous incremental archive. If a file has been moved to a different device (or the device number has changed), `tar` will emit a warning or error, helping you catch accidental cross‑device copies or storage migrations.

- With **`--no-check-device`**, `tar` skips this verification, which can be handy when you are sure the device numbers won’t change or when you want the backup to proceed without the extra check.

So, to **check** device numbers when creating incremental archives, just include `--check-device` (or rely on the default) on your `tar` command line.

           changed. Without a % sign, the number is to be read as a fraction, with a decimal point
           before it. I.e., -M5 becomes 0.5, and is thus the same as -M50%. Similarly, -M05 is the
           same as -M5%. To limit detection to exact renames, use -M100%. The default similarity
           index is 50%.

           has the same meaning as for -M<n>.

           the copy was modified in the same changeset. This flag makes the command inspect

           the same effect.

           preimage and /dev/null. The resulting patch is not meant to be applied with patch or git

           after the change. In addition, the output obviously lacks enough information to apply

           delete/create pair.

           renames/copies cheaply, followed by an exhaustive fallback portion that compares all
           remaining unpaired destinations to all relevant sources. (For renames, only remaining
           unpaired sources are relevant; for copies, all original sources are relevant.) For N
           sources and destinations, this exhaustive check is O(N^2). This option prevents the
           exhaustive portion of rename/copy detection from running if the number of
           source/destination files involved exceeds the specified number. Defaults to
           diff.renameLimit. Note that a value of 0 is treated as unlimited.

           Unmerged (U), are Unknown (X), or have had their pairing Broken (B). Any combination of

           the comparison; if there is no file that matches other criteria, nothing is selected.

Thus final answer.</think>`cargo clean` does **not** have a `--delete-source-code` option, and there is no built‑in flag with that name in the standard Cargo distribution.

### What `cargo clean` actually does
`cargo clean` removes the build artifacts that Cargo generates for the project, such as:

* The `target/` directory (compiled binaries, object files, etc.)
* Generated documentation (when `--doc` is used)
* Other intermediate files produced during compilation

It **does not** delete any of your source files (`*.rs`, `Cargo.toml`, etc.). The intent of `cargo clean` is to reset the build state so that a fresh compilation will start from scratch.

### Why the flag might be missing
- **Typo or confusion:** The help output for `cargo clean` (shown via `cargo clean --help`) lists only the options mentioned there (e.g., `--doc`, `-r/--release`, `-p/--package`, etc.). There is no `--delete-source-code`.
- **Older or custom wrappers:** Some third‑party scripts or older Cargo forks may have added a custom flag, but that would not be part of the official Cargo tool.
- **Different command:** If you want to remove source files, you would typically use a shell command like `rm -rf src/` or `git clean -fdx`, not a Cargo subcommand.

### If you need to delete source code
- **Manually:** Use `rm -rf path/to/source` (or your OS‑equivalent) to delete the files you no longer want.
- **Via Git:** `git clean -fdx` will remove untracked files (including source) from the working tree, but this operates on the filesystem, not through Cargo.
- **Re‑create the project:** `cargo new` can generate a fresh skeleton, after which you can copy over the source you wish to keep.

### Quick check
You can verify the available options yourself:

```bash
cargo clean --help
```

The output (as of the latest stable Cargo) does not contain `--delete-source-code`. If you encounter that flag in documentation or a script, it is likely a custom addition or a mis‑remembered option.

I'll respond.</think>The **`--print-type`** (short form **`-T`**) option tells `df` to include a column that shows the file‑system type for each listed mount point.

### Syntax

```bash
df -T          # short form
df --print-type   # long form
```

### What it does

- Adds a column named **`Type`** (or **`fstype`** when you use `--output`) that reports the filesystem type (e.g., `ext4`, `tmpfs`, `overlay`, `fusectl`, etc.).
- Works together with all the other `df` options (block‑size, human‑readable, filtering, etc.).

### Typical usage examples

```bash
# Show type column for all file systems
df -T
# Output (example)
Filesystem     1K-blocks    Used Available Use% Mounted on Type
/dev/sda1       20480000 5120000  15360000  26% /        ext4
/dev/sdb1       10240000 2048000  8192000  20% /data    xfs
tmpfs            409600       0   409600   0% /dev/shm tmpfs

# Combine with human‑readable sizes and a filter for a specific type
df -h -T -t ext4
# Show only ext4 file systems, with type column included

# Use --output to control exactly which columns appear
df --output=source,target,size,used,avail,type
```

### Quick cheat‑sheet

| Option | Long form | Effect |
|--------|-----------|--------|
| `-T`   | `--print-type` | Print the filesystem type column |
| `-t`   | `--type=TYPE`   | Limit listing to a specific type (e.g., `-t ext4`) |
| `-T` **and** `-t` | Both can be used together to filter *and* print the type |

So, to simply get the type information for every filesystem, run:

```bash
df --print-type
```

or

```bash
df -T
```

So answer: use journalctl -a --show-cursor or journalctl --all --show-cursor. Also maybe mention -o verbose etc. Provide example.</think>**Command**

```bash
journalctl -a --show-cursor
```

or equivalently

```bash
journalctl --all --show-cursor
```

**What the options do**

| Option | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| `-a` / `--all` | Show **all** fields for each entry, including long fields and unprintable (binary) data. Without this flag many fields are truncated or omitted. |
| `--show-cursor` | After the journal entries are printed, journalctl prints the **cursor** that marks the position of the last shown entry. This cursor can be saved (e.g., with `--cursor-file`) and later used with `--after-cursor` or `--cursor-file` to resume logging from that point. |

**Typical usage**

```bash
# Show everything that has been logged so far, with the cursor printed at the end
journalctl -a --show-cursor
```

If you want the cursor to be written to a file (so you can resume later), add `--cursor-file`:

```bash
journalctl -a --show-cursor --cursor-file=/path/to/cursor.txt
```

**Quick cheat‑sheet**

- `journalctl -a` → show all fields (long & unprintable)
- `journalctl --show-cursor` → print cursor after the entries
- `journalctl -a --show-cursor` → both together

Explain that docker stop only sends SIGTERM then SIGKILL, etc. If need to kill host power, that's outside docker's scope; you'd need to use host tools like ipmitool, etc. Provide guidance.</think>No. `docker stop` does not have a `--kill-node-power` (or any) option that can power‑off or reboot the underlying host machine.

`docker stop` only controls the **container** lifecycle:

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `-s, --signal` | Sends a specific signal (default `SIGTERM`) to the container’s main process |
| `-t, --timeout` | Seconds to wait after the signal before forcing a `SIGKILL` |

After the timeout (default 10 seconds) the container process is killed, but the host node continues running. Docker’s surface area does not include host‑level power management, because that would require privileged access to the host’s hardware/firmware and would be a security risk.

### What you can do instead

| Goal | How to achieve it |
|------|-------------------|
| **Gracefully stop a container** | `docker stop [container]` (or `docker container stop`) |
| **Forcefully kill a container** | `docker kill [container]` (sends `SIGKILL` immediately) |
| **Power‑off or reboot the host** | Use host‑level tools such as `systemctl poweroff`, `shutdown -h now`, IPMI commands (`ipmitool power off`), or your cloud provider’s API (e.g., AWS EC2 `stop-instances`, Azure `deallocate`, etc.). |
| **Combine container stop with host action** | Write a small script that first runs `docker stop` and then invokes the appropriate host command (e.g., `systemctl reboot`). |

If you need to automate a sequence (stop containers → power off host), you can script it:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Stop all running containers
docker stop $(docker ps -q)

# Then power off the host (requires appropriate privileges)
sudo systemctl poweroff   # or ipmitool power off, etc.
```

In short, `docker stop` cannot directly kill host node power; you’ll need to use host‑specific commands or APIs for that purpose.

The user asks: "Can you tell me the syntax for --no-check-device in tar?" We have the help output showing `--no-check-device` option description: "do not check device numbers when creating". We need to provide syntax. Likely the syntax is `--no-check-device` used with create mode (`-c`) or incremental backup. Provide usage: `tar --no-check-device -c archive.tar ...`. Might also need to mention it's used with incremental archives. Provide explanation.

Thus answer: The syntax is `--no-check-device`; you can use it as a standalone flag, typically alongside `-c` (create) or `-r` (append) etc. Provide example.

We'll answer.</think>**`--no-check-device`**  

```
tar [options] --no-check-device archive-name [files…]
```

- **What it does:**  
  When you are creating an *incremental* archive (e.g., with `-g`, `--listed-incremental`, or `-r`, `--append`), GNU tar normally checks the device numbers of the files against the device numbers stored in the archive’s header. If the device numbers differ, tar aborts with an error.  
  Adding `--no-check-device` tells tar **not** to perform that check, so the archive can be created even when the files reside on a different device (or when the device number cannot be determined).

- **Typical usage:**  

  ```bash
  # Create a level‑0 incremental archive without device‑number checking
  tar -c --no-check-device -f full-backup.tar /home /var

  # Append new files to an existing incremental archive without device‑number checking
  tar -r --no-check-device -f full-backup.tar /home/new
  ```

- **Common options it’s used with:**  
  `-c, --create` – create a new archive  
  `-r, --append` – append files to an existing archive  
  `-g, --listed-incremental=FILE` – GNU‑format incremental backup  
  `-G, --incremental` – old‑format incremental backup  

- **Why you might need it:**  
  - Moving an archive between systems where the device node (e.g., `/dev/sda1`) differs.  
  - Backing up files from a container or a ramdisk where a device number isn’t meaningful.  
  - Automating backups in environments where device numbers can change between runs.

In short, the syntax is simply the flag `--no-check-device` placed on the `tar` command line, usually together with a create/append operation.

We have the answer. Provide syntax and explanation.</think>The **`--all`** (or **`-a`**) flag for `docker images` tells Docker to show **all images**, including intermediate and dangling images that are normally hidden.

### Basic syntax

```bash
docker images [OPTIONS] [REPOSITORY[:TAG]]
```

### Using `--all` / `-a`

```bash
# Show every image on the host (including dangling/intermediate ones)
docker images --all

# Short form
docker images -a
```

### What changes

| Behaviour | Without `--all` | With `--all` (`-a`) |
|-----------|----------------|--------------------|
| **User‑created images** | Shown | Shown |
| **Official/base images** (e.g., `ubuntu`, `nginx`) | Shown | Shown |
| **Intermediate images** (created during `docker build`) | Hidden | Shown |
| **Dangling images** (`<none>`, `<none>`) | Hidden | Shown |
| **Tag column** | May be `<none>` for dangling images | Still `<none>`, but the image appears in the list |

### Common optional combos

```bash
# Show all images, but only their IDs (quiet mode)
docker images -aq

# Show all images with their digests
docker images --all --digests

# Format the output (e.g., JSON)
docker images --all --format "{{json .}}"
```

### Quick cheat‑sheet

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `-a`, `--all` | List **all** images (default hides intermediate/dangling) |
| `-q`, `--quiet` | Print only image IDs |
| `--digests` | Include image digest (hash) in output |
| `--filter` | Filter by criteria (`dangling=true`, `reference=…`, etc.) |
| `--format` | Use a Go template to customise output |

So, to see everything Docker has stored locally, just run:

```bash
docker images -a
```

We have the answer: -t, --tty allocate a pseudo-TTY. We can explain what it does: connects a terminal, enables interactive features, etc. Provide context.</think>**`--tty` (short form: `-t`)** tells Docker to allocate a **pseudo‑terminal (PTY)** for the command you run inside the container.

### What that actually does

| Effect | Explanation |
|--------|-------------|
| **Terminal emulation** | The container’s standard input/output behaves like a real terminal. Programs that check for a TTY (e.g., `less`, `top`, `vim`, `script`) will see a proper terminal device instead of a plain pipe. |
| **ANSI‑escape handling** | Colour codes, cursor movement, and other escape sequences are interpreted by the shell/application rather than being printed literally. |
| **Larger input buffer** | The PTY provides a line‑buffered input, so commands that read input line‑by‑line (e.g., `read` in bash) work as they would on a real console. |
| **Job control** | You can use `Ctrl‑C`, `Ctrl‑Z`, and other job‑control signals inside the container, just as you would on a local terminal. |
| **Interactive prompts** | Many programs that ask for input or display a prompt will present a proper cursor and prompt line. |

### Typical usage

```bash
# Start an interactive bash shell with a TTY
docker exec -it my_container bash

# Or just the TTY flag (without -i)
docker exec -t my_container top
```

- **`-i` (--interactive)** keeps STDIN open, but does **not** allocate a PTY.
- **`-t` (--tty)** allocates a PTY.  
- Using **both `-i` and `-t`** (`-it`) gives you a fully interactive session (you can type, see prompts, use arrow keys, etc.).

### When you’d want it

- Running **interactive programs** (`vim`, `htop`, `mysql`, `psql`, etc.).
- Debugging scripts that need terminal‑style input/output.
- Any situation where the application relies on detecting `isatty()` or processing ANSI escape sequences.

### When you might not need it

- Running a simple one‑line command that only prints output (e.g., `docker exec my_container echo hello`).
- Running background/daemon‑style processes where you don’t need a terminal interface.

In short, `--tty` makes the executed command think it’s running on a real terminal, enabling proper terminal features and interactive behavior inside the container.

We should not need more tools. We'll answer.</think>`docker stop` does **not** have a `--kill-node-power` (or any “‑kill‑node‑power”) option.  

The `docker stop` command only supports a few very simple options:

```
Usage: docker stop [OPTIONS] CONTAINER [CONTAINER...]

Options:
  -s, --signal string   Signal to send to the container (default: SIGTERM)
  -t, --timeout int     Seconds to wait before killing the container
```

So a command like

```
docker stop --kill-node-power <container>
```

will fail with an “unknown flag: --kill-node-power” error.

---

### What to do instead

If your run‑book intends to power‑off the physical host that a container runs on, that is **outside the scope of Docker**. Docker can only stop or kill containers; it has no direct control over host‑level power management.

Typical ways to power‑off or reboot a host are:

| Method | Typical command / tool |
|--------|------------------------|
| **IPMI / BMC** | `ipmitool -I lanplus -H <host> -U <user> power off` |
| **iDRAC / iLO** | `racadm -r <host> -u <user> -p <pass> power cycle` |
| **systemctl / shutdown** (if you have shell access) | `sudo systemctl poweroff` or `sudo shutdown -h now` |
| **Wake‑on‑LAN / remote power‑on** | `wakeonlan <mac>` (to turn it back on) |

If the goal is simply to **force‑stop** the container (equivalent to a SIGKILL), you can use:

```bash
docker stop -s SIGKILL <container>
```

or, more simply:

```bash
docker kill <container>
```

`docker kill` sends a SIGKILL immediately, whereas `docker stop` first sends SIGTERM and waits for the timeout.

---

### Summary

- `docker stop --kill-node-power` is not a valid Docker flag.
- Use `docker stop` (or `docker kill`) to stop containers.
- To power‑off the underlying host, rely on host‑level management tools (IPMI, iDRAC, `systemctl`, etc.).

| Option | Shorthand | What it does |

### Basic usage

```bash
# or
```

| Command | Effect |
|---------|--------|

### Basic syntax

```bash
git diff --stat [<options>] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
```

or, more compactly, you can combine it with other diff options:

```bash
git diff --stat -p   # show both the stat summary and the patch
git diff --stat --cached   # show stats for the staging area
```

### What it prints

When you use `--stat`, the output looks like this:

```
 README.md | 10 ++++---- 2 files changed, 6 insertions(+), 4 deletions(-)
```

- The first line(s) give a **diffstat** – a compact line‑by‑line summary of how many lines were added (`+`) and deleted (`‑`) per file.
- After the stat lines, Git may still show the **total** number of files changed, insertions, and deletions.
- If you also use `-p` or `--patch-with-stat`, the patch itself is shown **preceded** by the stat summary for each file.

### Common useful variants

| Variant | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `git diff --stat` | Shows only the diffstat summary (no patch). |
| `git diff --numstat` | Shows numeric insert/delete counts per file (e.g., `10\t5\t2`). |
| `git diff --patch-with-stat` | Shows the patch **and** a stat line prepended to each file’s diff. |
| `git diff --stat --cached` | Shows stats for changes that are staged but not yet committed. |
| `git diff --stat --no-index` | Useful for comparing two arbitrary files or directories that are not under Git control. |

### Typical use‑case

If you just want a quick overview of how many lines changed and which files were touched—without the full text diff—`--stat` is the go‑to flag:

```bash
git diff --stat HEAD~5 HEAD
```

Output example:

```
 Documentation/foo.txt | 3 ++-
 Documentation/bar.c  | 10 ++++----
 2 files changed, 7 insertions(+), 3 deletions(-)
```

That tells you at a glance that two files were modified, with a net total of 7 added lines and 3 removed lines.

### Quick checklist

- **Show stat only:** `git diff --stat`
- **Stat + patch:** `git diff --patch-with-stat`
- **Numeric stat:** `git diff --numstat`
- **Stat for staged changes:** `git diff --stat --cached`

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| **`-6, --ipv6`** | **Use IPv6 addresses only** when contacting the remote. If the remote has both IPv4 and IPv6 endpoints, this forces Git to prefer (or exclusively use) the IPv6 address. |
| **`--unshallow`** | **Convert a shallow repository into a complete one**. After fetching with this flag, any shallow‑clone depth limits are removed and the full history is fetched. |

### Combined command

```bash
git fetch -6 --unshallow <remote> [<refspec>…]
```

- `-6` → “use IPv6 only”.
- `--unshallow` → “make the repository complete (remove shallow constraints)”.

You can also write it as:

```bash
git fetch --ipv6 --unshallow <remote> [<refspec>…]
```

### Quick note on usage

- If you just want to *inspect* the effect without actually transferring data, add `--dry-run` (or `-n` for “no‑fetch”):
  ```bash
  git fetch -6 --unshallow --dry-run origin
  ```
- If you’re fetching from multiple remotes, you can repeat the flags or use `git fetch --multiple -6 --unshallow <remote1> <remote2> …`.

- **What it does:** Moves the current `HEAD` to the specified `<commit>` **without** touching the working‑tree files or the staging area (index).  
- **Default `<commit>`:** If you omit the commit, `HEAD` is used.  
- **Typical use‑case:** Combine several recent commits into one, e.g.:

```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~5   # move HEAD back 5 commits
git commit -m "combined 5 commits"
```

- **Effect on state:**

| Area                | After `git reset --soft` |
|---------------------|--------------------------|
| **HEAD**            | Points to the new commit |

We have the answer: -M detects renames, -p outputs patch format. So we can combine: git diff -M -p or git diff -p -M. Also can use --stat etc. Provide explanation.</think>`git diff` lets you control two things you asked about:

| Goal | Option | What it does |
|------|--------|--------------|
| **Detect renames** | `-M` | tells Git to look for files that have been renamed (as opposed to just showing them as deleted + added). |
| **Output patch format** | `-p` (or `-u`) | produces a unified‑diff patch that shows the actual line‑by‑line changes, prefixed with `---`/`+++` headers and `+`/`-` markers. |

### Typical command

```bash
git diff -M -p   # (or equivalently: git diff -p -M)
```

- `-M` enables rename detection.
- `-p` (or `-u`) emits the patch‑style diff.

### Other useful flags you might combine

| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--stat` | Shows a brief statistics line (files changed, insertions/deletions) above the patch. |
| `--patch-with-stat` | Emits the patch **and** the statistics line. |
| `--name-only` / `--name-status` | Lists only the changed file names (or names + status letters). |
| `-B` | Detects “complete rewrites” (a file that changed so much it’s treated as a new file). |
| `-C` | Also detects copies, not just renames. |
| `--find-copies-harder` | Makes the copy/rename detection look at unchanged files as candidates too. |

### Quick demo

```bash
# Show a patch that highlights renames
git diff -M -p HEAD~5 HEAD
```

If you want the patch **and** a diff‑raw view of the raw line changes, you can use:

```bash
git diff --patch-with-raw -M -p HEAD~5 HEAD
```

That will give you the unified patch (`-p`) plus the raw diff lines (`--patch-with-raw`), and `-M` will still flag any renames.

Provide answer.</think>The **`-F`** (or **`--fixed-strings`**) option tells `grep` to treat the pattern(s) as plain **literals** rather than regular expressions.  

### Basic syntax

```bash
grep [OPTION]... -F PATTERN [FILE]...
# or
grep [OPTION]... --fixed-strings PATTERN [FILE]...
```

### What it does

| Feature | Without `-F` | With `-F` / `--fixed-strings` |
|---------|--------------|--------------------------------|
| Pattern type | Regular expression (e.g., `.` matches any character, `*` repeats) | Plain string (literal match) |
| Metacharacters | Interpreted as regex syntax | Treated as ordinary characters |
| Speed | May be slower for complex patterns | Generally faster because no regex engine is needed |

### Common examples

```bash
# Search for the literal text "error" (no regex interpretation)
grep -F "error" log.txt

# Search for multiple literal strings (each on a new line in the pattern file)
grep -F -f patterns.txt data.txt

# Case‑insensitive literal match
grep -Fi -F "warning" syslog.txt

# Show line numbers and treat the pattern as a fixed string
grep -n -F "path/to/file" *.conf
```

### Quick checklist

- **`-F`** or **`--fixed-strings`** → patterns are literal strings.
- **`-E`** (or **`--extended-regexp`**) → patterns are extended regular expressions (the default when you just type a pattern).
- **`-G`** (or **`--basic-regexp`**) → patterns are basic regular expressions.
- Use `-F` when you need exact, fast string matching and want to avoid having to escape regex metacharacters like `.`, `*`, `?`, `[`, `]`, etc.

Also `-m` moves/renames but will error if target exists. So answer: `-M` or `--move`. Provide explanation.</think>The option you’re looking for is **`-M`** (or equivalently **`--move`**).

```bash
git branch -M <old-branch> <new-branch>
```

- `-M` **moves/renames** the branch to the new name.  
- If the target branch name already exists, `-M` will **force the rename** (it removes the existing target first).  

For comparison:

| Option | Behaviour |
|--------|------------|
| `-m` / `--move` | Move/rename the branch **unless** the target already exists (will error if it does). |
| `-M` / `--move` | Move/rename the branch **even if** the target exists (forces the rename). |
| `-c` / `--copy` | Copy the branch and its reflog; `-C` copies even if the target exists. |
| `-d` / `-D` | Delete a branch (merged or not). |

So, to rename a branch regardless of whether the destination already exists, use `git branch -M`.

Why does my dog dig in the furniture?

Most dogs were originally bred to service a function.  Some dogs were bred to chase small animals, for hunting rabbits or fox.  Many of these breeds were also intended to dig for their kills, so your dog may burrow because it's born to do that.  Said differently, some terrier breeds were meant to hunt rats, i.e. the rat terrier.  These dogs will dig even if there is nothing to dig for simply because it's what they were bred to do.  Other dogs dig to create nesting areas, to warm up their area before they lay down, or to check for bugs.

Thus respond.</think>In `git branch` the flag that copies a branch **even if the target already exists** is **`-C`** (or equivalently `--copy` with the “force” semantics).  

- `-c` / `--copy` – copies a branch and its reflog, but will fail if the target branch already exists.  
- `-C` / `--copy` – copies a branch and its reflog, **overwriting** the target if it already exists.

```bash
git branch -C <new-branch> <start-point>
```

</think>To display **only the journal entries belonging to the current user**, run:

```bash
journalctl --user
```

(You can also use the short form `journalctl -u`; `-u` alone means “user units”, but adding `--user` (or `-u` with no unit name) explicitly switches to the user journal.)

### Common useful variants

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| Show the last N lines of the user journal | `journalctl --user -n 50` |
| Follow the user journal in real time | `journalctl --user -f` |
| Show entries since a certain time (e.g., “today”) | `journalctl --user -S today` |
| Show entries until a certain time | `journalctl --user -U "2025‑08‑31 23:59"` |
| Combine with a unit filter (e.g., only `docker.service` for the user) | `journalctl --user -u docker.service` |
| Output in JSON for scripting | `journalctl --user -o json` |

### Quick tip

If you often need the user journal, you can create an alias:

```bash
alias juser='journalctl --user'
```

Then simply typing `juser` (or `juser -n 20` etc.) will show the current‑user’s journal.

messages.content:
GIT-TAG(1)                                   Git Manual                                  GIT-TAG(1)

NAME
       git-tag - Create, list, delete or verify tags

SYNOPSIS
       git tag [-a | -s | -u <key-id>] [-f] [-m <msg> | -F <file>] [-e]
               [(--trailer <token>[(=|:)<value>])...]
               <tagname> [<commit> | <object>]
       git tag -d <tagname>...
       git tag [-n[<num>]] -l [--contains <commit>] [--no-contains <commit>]
               [--points-at <object>] [--column[=<options>] | --no-column]
               [--create-reflog] [--sort=<key>] [--format=<format>]
               [--merged <commit>] [--no-merged <commit>] [<pattern>...]
       git tag -v [--format=<format>] <tagname>...

DESCRIPTION
       Add a tag reference in refs/tags/, unless -d/-l/-v is given to delete, list or verify tags.

       Unless -f is given, the named tag must not yet exist.

       If one of -a, -s, or -u <key-id> is passed, the command creates a tag object, and requires a
       tag message. Unless -m <msg> or -F <file> is given, an editor is started for the user to
       type in the tag message.

       If -m <msg> or -F <file> or --trailer <token>[=<value>] is given and -a, -s, and -u <key-id>
       are absent, -a is implied.

       Otherwise, a tag reference that points directly at the given object (i.e., a lightweight
       tag) is created.

       A cryptographically signed tag object will be created when -s or -u <key-id> is used. The
       signing backend (GPG, X.509, SSH, etc.) is controlled by the gpg.format configuration
       variable, defaulting to OpenPGP. When -u <key-id> is not used, the committer identity for
       the current user is used to find the key for signing. The configuration variable gpg.program
       is used to specify a custom signing binary.

       Tag objects (created with -a, -s, or -u) are called "annotated" tags; they contain a
       creation date, the tagger name and e-mail, a tagging message, and an optional cryptographic
       signature. Whereas a "lightweight" tag is simply a name for an object (usually a commit
       object).

       Annotated tags are meant for release while lightweight tags are meant for private or
       temporary object labels. For this reason, some git commands for naming objects (like git
       describe) will ignore lightweight tags by default.

```
git tag [options] <tagname> [<commit> | <object>]
```

The `--trailer` option lets you add one or more “trailer” lines to the tag message.  
Its syntax is:

```
--trailer <token>[(=|:)<value>]
```

* **`<token>`** – the name of the trailer (e.g., `Signed-off-by`, `Reviewed-by`, `Co-authored-by`, …).  
* **`(=|:)<value>`** – optional assignment of a value to that token.  
  * `=` or `:` separates the token from its value.  
  * If you omit the `=`/`:` and the value, the trailer is recorded with an empty value (just the token name).  

You can repeat the option as many times as you need:

```
git tag --trailer "Signed-off-by=John Doe" --trailer "Reviewed-by: Jane Smith" v1.2
```

or, using the short form without a value:

```
git tag --trailer "Signed-off-by" v1.2
```

**Typical usage**

```bash
git tag -a v1.2.3 \
    -m "Release notes" \
    --trailer "Signed-off-by=Alice <alice@example.com>" \
    --trailer "Reviewed-by=Bob <bob@example.com>" \
    HEAD
```

This creates an annotated tag `v1.2.3` whose message contains the usual `-m` text **plus** the two trailer lines:

```
Release notes

Signed-off-by: Alice <alice@example.com>
Reviewed-by: Bob <bob@example.com>
```

The `--trailer` flag is just another way to add key‑value pairs to the tag annotation, and it works whether you use `-a`, `-s`, or `-u` (annotated/signing) or create a lightweight tag.

I'll answer.</think>Git diff can output its result in **patch format** (the unified diff that shows `+`/`-` lines, headers, etc.).  
The simplest way is to add the `-p` (or its synonym `-u`) option.

```bash
# Show a patch for the working‑tree changes
git diff -p

# Show a patch comparing two specific commits/tag/branches
git diff -p <commit1> <commit2>

# Show a patch for the staged (index) changes only
git diff -p --cached
```

### What the flag does

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `-p` | Output the diff in **patch format** (the default unified‑diff style). |
| `-u` | Synonym for `-p`; also outputs patch format. |
| `--patch` | Another synonym (newer Git versions). |
| `-R` | (optional) reverse the diff (swap the two sides). |

### Example outputs

**Basic patch for unstaged changes**

```bash
$ git diff -p
diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
index 3c2e1e2..9f1a5b3 100644
--- a/README.md
+++ b/README.md
@@ -1,4 +1,5 @@
 # My Project
 
+A new line of documentation.
   Other content...
```

**Patch comparing two branches**

```bash
$ git diff -p main..feature-x
diff --git a/src/utils.py b/src/utils.py
...
```

**Patch for staged changes only**

```bash
$ git diff -p --cached
```

### Quick tip

If you want the patch **and** the raw diff (the exact byte‑wise changes), you can combine options:

```bash
git diff --patch-with-raw   # shows both the patch and the -z raw format
```

That’s all you need – just add `-p` (or `-u`/`--patch`) to `git diff` and you’ll get a patch‑format output.

Thus answer.</think>The **`--list`** (or **`-t`**) option tells `tar` to display the names of the files that are stored in an archive — it does **not** extract them.

### Basic syntax

```bash
tar [options] --list [archive]
```

or, using the short form:

```bash
tar -t [options] [archive]
```

### Commonly used options with `--list`

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `-f, --file=ARCHIVE` | Specify the archive file (if you don’t use a default tape device). |
| `-v, --verbose` | Show additional information (e.g., file size, permissions, modification time). |
| `-v` combined with `-t` | `tar -tvf archive.tar` → verbose listing. |
| `--ignore-failed-read` | Don’t report an error if a file inside the archive can’t be read. |
| `--no-seek` | useful for non‑seekable streams (e.g., piping). |

### Typical examples

1. **List the contents of an archive (short form)**  

   ```bash
   tar -t -f myarchive.tar
   ```

2. **List the contents with verbose details (sizes, dates, permissions)**  

   ```bash
   tar -tvf myarchive.tar
   ```

3. **List only files that match a pattern**  

   ```bash
   tar -t --exclude='*.tmp' -f myarchive.tar
   ```

4. **List the contents of a compressed archive (gzip)**  

   ```bash
   tar -tzf myarchive.tar.gz
   ```

### Quick cheat‑sheet

| Command | Effect |
|---------|--------|
| `tar -t archive.tar` | List file names only. |
| `tar -tvf archive.tar` | List with verbose info (size, date, permissions). |
| `tar --list -f archive.tar.gz` | Same as `-t` but explicit long form. |
| `tar -tzf archive.tar.gz` | List contents of a gzip‑compressed archive. |

In short, the syntax is simply `tar -t [options] archive` (or `tar --list [options] archive`). The option’s primary purpose is to inspect what’s inside an archive without modifying the filesystem.

**What `cargo clean` actually does**

```
cargo clean [options]
```

- Removes the artifacts that Cargo generated for the selected package/workspace:
  - `target/` directory (compiled binaries, object files, etc.)
  - Documentation that was generated with `cargo doc`
  - Other build‑cache files

It **never** touches the source files in `src/` or the `Cargo.toml`.

**Why the flag doesn’t exist**

Cargo’s design philosophy is to keep source code under your control. Deleting source code would be destructive and could lead to accidental loss of work, so the tool deliberately omits any option that would do that.

**If you really want to delete the source code**

You’ll have to do it yourself with a regular shell command, e.g.:

```bash
# Remove the whole project directory (use with extreme care!)
rm -rf /path/to/your/project

# Or just delete the source files while keeping the Cargo.toml, etc.
rm -rf /path/to/your/project/src
```

**Typical workflow**

1. **Clean build artifacts** (safe, won’t touch source):

   ```bash
   cargo clean
   ```

2. **Rebuild from scratch**:

   ```bash
   cargo build
   ```

3. **If you need a completely fresh start** (including source), back up whatever you want to keep, then delete the directory and re‑clone/checkout the repo.

**Summary**

- You can’t run `cargo clean --delete-source-code` because the flag doesn’t exist.
- `cargo clean` only removes generated artifacts, not source code.
- To delete source code, use ordinary shell commands (e.g., `rm -rf …`), but be very careful because that action is irreversible.

We need to answer: "With git tag, how do I print only tags that are merged, and also print only tags that contain the commit?" So we need to explain using --merged and --contains options. Possibly combine them. Provide examples.

We can answer directly; no need for more tool usage. Provide commands:

git tag --merged <commit> lists tags merged into that commit (default HEAD). git tag --contains <commit> lists tags that contain the commit.

Explain usage.

Will answer.</think>`git tag` has two dedicated options that do exactly what you’re asking for.

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| **`--merged <commit>`** | Prints **only** the tags that are *merged* into the named commit (i.e. the commit (or its ancestors) is reachable from the tag). If you omit `<commit>` it defaults to the current HEAD. |
| **`--contains <commit>`** | Prints **only** the tags that *contain* the named commit (the commit is reachable from the tag). Again, HEAD is used if you leave the argument blank. |

You can use them together (or separately) to filter the tag list any way you need.

---

### 1. Show only tags that are merged into a commit

```bash
# merged into HEAD (the default)
git tag --merged

# merged into a specific commit, e.g. v2.3.1
git tag --merged v2.3.1
```

The command will list every tag whose tip commit is an ancestor of the given commit – i.e. the tag’s history includes that commit.

---

### 2. Show only tags that contain a commit

```bash
# tags that contain HEAD
git tag --contains

# tags that contain a particular commit hash or name
git tag --contains abc1234
```

Here the output is limited to tags whose own history includes the specified commit.

---

### 3. Combine both filters (tags that are **both** merged **and** contain a commit)

```bash
git tag --merged --contains <commit>
```

- `--merged` first narrows the list to tags that are merged.
- `--contains` then further narrows it to only those that also contain the named commit.

If you leave out the commit argument, both flags default to `HEAD`, so `git tag --merged --contains` will show tags that are merged into HEAD **and** also contain HEAD (which, for a linear history, will usually be just the HEAD tag itself).

---

### Quick examples

```bash
# List tags merged into the current branch tip
git tag --merged

# List tags that contain the commit that introduced a bug fix
git tag --contains abcdef123

# Show tags that are merged into v2.4.0 **and** also contain that same tag
git tag --merged --contains v2.4.0
```

---

### TL;DR

- `git tag --merged <commit>` → tags merged into `<commit>`.
- `git tag --contains <commit>` → tags that contain `<commit>`.
- Use them together: `git tag --merged --contains <commit>` to get tags that satisfy **both** conditions.

From the help: `-b` creates a new branch, `-B` creates or resets if exists. So answer: use `git checkout -b <new-branch>` to create and checkout, or `git checkout -B <branch>` to create or reset (force). Provide explanation.

Thus respond.</think>Git’s `checkout` command has a couple of options that let you both **create** a new branch and **switch to it** in one step:

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| **`-b <new‑branch>`** | Creates the branch *if it doesn’t exist* and then checks it out. If the branch already exists, Git will refuse (unless you also use `-f`). |
| **`-B <branch>`** | Creates the branch *or* resets it to the given start‑point if it already exists. This is equivalent to `git checkout -b` **but** it will succeed even when the branch name is already taken, forcing a reset to the start point. |

### Typical usage

- **Create a new branch and switch to it**  
  ```bash
  git checkout -b <new-branch>
  ```

- **Create (or reset) a branch and switch to it** – useful when you want to guarantee a fresh start, even if the branch already exists:  
  ```bash
  git checkout -B <branch>
  ```

- **Specify a start point** (optional) – you can tell Git where the new branch should begin, e.g. a specific commit, tag, or another branch:  
  ```bash
  git checkout -b <new-branch> <start-point>
  git checkout -B <branch> <start-point>
  ```

### Quick cheat‑sheet

- `git checkout -b <branch>` → create + checkout (fails if branch already exists)  
- `git checkout -B <branch>` → create or reset + checkout (always succeeds)  

So, depending on whether you want the command to error out when the branch name is already taken, pick **`-b`** (create‑only) or **`-B`** (create‑or‑reset).

**Typical usage**

```bash
git diff -u   # same as git diff -p
```

You can also combine it with other options, e.g.:

```bash
git diff -u --stat   # patch + short statistics
```

- Other related options:

### The one‑liner

```bash
docker ps -q -s
```

or, using the long form:

```bash
docker ps --quiet --size
```

### What you’ll see

```
3b5c2a9e8f1a
a1d2e3f4b5c6
...
```

If you also want the size column printed **beside** the IDs (instead of on a separate line), you can use the `--format` flag to cherry‑pick the fields you need:

```bash
docker ps -q --format "{{.ID}} {{.Size}}"
```

That will output something like:

```
3b5c2a9e8f1a  1.2GB
a1d2e3f4b5c6  850MB
```

### Quick recap

- **`-q`** → container IDs only.  
- **`-s`** → show total file sizes.  
- **`-q -s`** (or **`--quiet --size`**) → both in a single `docker ps` command.

So answer: git diff -C --numstat. Provide explanation.</think>Git lets you combine those two behaviours in a single `git diff` invocation.

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| **`-C`** | Detects **copies** as well as renames. Without `-C` a file that was copied and then modified would appear as a deletion + addition; with `-C` Git reports it as a copy. |
| **`--numstat`** | Shows a **numeric diffstat** (added/removed line counts) instead of the full patch text. It prints three columns: `<added> <deleted> <file>` for each changed path. |

### The combined command

```bash
git diff -C --numstat <commit‑range> -- <path‑spec>
```

- `-C` → copy‑detection.
- `--numstat` → numeric diffstat (no patch output).

You can also add other handy flags, e.g.:

- `--stat` → a human‑readable diffstat (adds/deletes/total) *and* the patch; if you only want the numeric version, `--numstat` is the one to use.
- `-M` → rename detection (if you also want rename detection, you can use `-C -M`; `-C` already implies rename detection, but `-M` makes it explicit).
- `--no-index` → useful for comparing two arbitrary files/folders that aren’t under Git’s control.

### Quick test

```bash
git diff -C --numstat HEAD~5 HEAD -- src/
```

This will:

1. Show any files that were **copied** (or renamed) between the two commits.
2. Print a numeric diffstat for each changed file, e.g.:

```
 12   5  src/main.c
  3   0  src/utils.h
```

instead of the usual unified diff patch.

```bash
docker run --init my-image
```

If you need to customise the init binary or completely replace the entrypoint, you can also use `--entrypoint` together with `--init`, but `--init` itself is the flag that tells Docker to run an init process inside the container.

The -name-only shows only names. -C detects copies. So answer.</think>**One‑liner**

```bash
git diff -C --name-only   # (or: git diff --name-only -C)
```

* `-C` – detect copies (as well as renames).  
* `--name-only` – list only the names of the changed files, omitting the actual diff text.

---

### Why this works

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `-C`   | Enables copy detection.  Git will report a file as “copied” ( `A → B` ) if the same content exists elsewhere in the tree, even if the file was also modified. |
| `--name-only` | Suppresses the patch output and prints just the file names (one per line). |
| Combining them | Gives you a concise list of files, but any file that Git recognises as a copy (or rename) will be marked accordingly. |

If you also want to detect **complete rewrites** (i.e., a file that was deleted and a new file with similar content added), you can add `-B`:

```bash
git diff -C -B --name-only
```

Or, if you want the extra “harder” copy detection that also looks at unchanged files as candidates, use `--find-copies-harder`:

```bash
git diff --name-only -C --find-copies-harder
```

---

### Quick test

```bash
# Show only names, flagging copies
git diff -C --name-only
```

You’ll see output like:

```
src/main.py
src/utils.py   (copied from src/old_utils.py)
README.md
```

The second line indicates that `src/utils.py` was detected as a copy of `src/old_utils.py`.

           "USER_INVOCATION_ID=".

           the journal, and zero or a negative offset will look up invocations starting from the
           end of the journal. Thus, 1 means the first invocation found in the journal in
           chronological order, 2 the second and so on; while 0 is the latest invocation, -1 the
           invocation before the latest, and so on.

           identifies the invocation relative to the one given by invocation ID. Negative values
           mean earlier invocations and positive values mean later invocations. If ±offset is not
           specified, a value of zero is assumed, and the logs for the invocation given by ID will
           be shown.

Might also mention that it's used to customize mapping of remote refs to local refs. Provide typical usage.</think>`git fetch` accepts a **`--refmap`** option that lets you specify a *refmap* – a string that tells Git how to map the remote’s references to local references.

### Syntax

```bash
git fetch --refmap <refmap> [<repository> [<refspec>...]]
```

* `<refmap>` – a **refmap** expression that describes the mapping between remote refs and local refs.  
  The format is a comma‑separated list of **`src:dst`** pairs, where:

  * `src` – the source reference on the remote (e.g., `refs/heads/main`).
  * `dst` – the destination reference where the objects will be stored locally (e.g., `refs/remotes/origin/main`).

  If you omit the `dst` part, the remote ref is stored under the same name under `refs/remotes/`.

### Common examples

| Command | Effect |
|---------|--------|
| `git fetch --refmap "refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*"` | Maps every remote head `refs/heads/*` to `refs/remotes/origin/*`. |
| `git fetch --refmap "refs/heads/main:refs/heads/my-main"` | Fetches the remote `main` branch and stores it locally as `my-main`. |
| `git fetch --refmap "refs/tags/*:refs/tags/*"` | Copies all tags from the remote, preserving their names. |
| `git fetch --refmap ""` | (empty refmap) – fetches the default set of refs (the repository’s default refspec). |

### How it works

When you use `--refmap`, Git **overwrites** the default refspec that would normally be generated from the remote’s `refs/heads/` and `refs/tags/` namespaces. The refmap you supply determines exactly which remote refs end up where in your local repository (usually under `refs/remotes/` or directly as local branches, depending on the `dst` part).

### Quick tip

If you just want to see what the current default refspec would be (without any custom mapping), you can run:

```bash
git fetch   # shows the default refspecs in the output
```

or

```bash
git config -l | grep fetch
```

to inspect the repository’s `fetch` configuration.

---

**In short:**  

```bash
git fetch --refmap "<src>:<dst>,<src2>:<dst2>" <remote>
```

uses the supplied refmap instead of the auto‑generated one, giving you fine‑grained control over which remote references are fetched and where they are stored locally.

Thus answer: use `docker exec -d -u root <container> <command>` or `docker exec --detach --user root <container> <command>`. Also mention that to give extended privileges you typically need to start the container with `--privileged` or run `sudo` inside.

So answer: use -d and --privileged together. Provide example command.</think>Both of those flags can be used together in a single `docker exec` invocation.

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **`-d`, `--detach`** | Run the command in detached mode (the container’s process starts in the background). |
| **`--privileged`** | Give the command extended (root‑level) privileges inside the container. |

### Example


Running the command above will start `<command>` inside the specified container, detach from it, and give that command elevated privileges—all in one `docker exec` call.

```bash
tar --delete -f archive.tar file1 file2 ...
```

We have the answer from docker exec --help. The --interactive (short -i) flag keeps STDIN open even if not attached. So we can explain.</think>The **`--interactive`** (or `-i`) flag for `docker exec` tells Docker to keep the container’s standard input (STDIN) open, even if the command is not currently attached to a terminal.

**What this means in practice**

| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `-i` / `--interactive` | Keeps STDIN open. If you later attach (e.g., with `docker attach` or `docker exec -i -t …`), the process will see input coming from your terminal. Without it, the process receives EOF immediately. |
| `-t` / `--tty` | Allocates a pseudo‑TTY (a terminal). This is usually used together with `-i` to get an interactive shell. |
| `-i` **without** `-t` | The command’s stdin stays open, but no terminal device is allocated, so you won’t get a interactive prompt (e.g., line editing, colors). It’s useful when you just need to pipe input into the command. |

**Typical usage**

```bash
# Run an interactive shell inside a container (needs both -i and -t)
docker exec -it my_container bash

# Run a command that reads from stdin, keeping stdin open
docker exec -i my_container cat > output.txt
```

In short, `--interactive` ensures that the container’s STDIN isn’t closed just because you aren’t currently attached to the session, allowing the command to receive input later (e.g., via a pipe or when you re‑attach).

They might want description. Provide explanation: `--refresh` refreshes the index after reset, etc. Provide usage.</think>`git reset` accepts a `--refresh` flag (its opposite is `--no-refresh`).  

**Syntax**

```bash
git reset [--refresh] [<commit>]
# or
git reset [--refresh] [<tree-ish>] [--] <pathspec>...
# or
git reset [--refresh] [--patch [<tree-ish>] [--] [<pathspec>...]]
```

**What it does**

- `--refresh` tells Git to refresh the index (i.e., update the staging area) after the reset operation, ensuring that any changes that would be overwritten are kept in the index rather than being lost.
- By default (`--no-refresh`, which is the default behavior), the index is **not** refreshed; any files that would be overwritten are simply reset to the state recorded in the target commit.

In practice, `--refresh` is rarely needed because the default behavior already refreshes the index when appropriate, but you can explicitly use it if you want to make the intent clear or override a `--no-refresh` setting.

NAME

SYNOPSIS

               [--merged <commit>] [--no-merged <commit>] [<pattern>...]
       git tag -v [--format=<format>] <tagname>...

DESCRIPTION
       Add a tag reference in refs/tags/, unless -d/-l/-v is given to delete, list or verify tags.

       Unless -f is given, the named tag must not yet exist.

       If one of -a, -s, or -u <key-id> is passed, the command creates a tag object, and requires a
       tag message. Unless -m <msg> or -F <file> is given, an editor is started for the user to
       type in the tag message.

       If -m <msg> or -F <file> or --trailer <token>[=<value>] is given and -a, -s, and -u <key-id>
       are absent, -a is implied.

       Otherwise, a tag reference that points directly at the given object (i.e., a lightweight
       tag) is created.

       A cryptographically signed tag object will be created when -s or -u <key-id> is used. The
       signing backend (GPG, X.509, SSH, etc.) is controlled by the gpg.format configuration
       variable, defaulting to OpenPGP. When -u <key-id> is not used, the committer identity for
       the current user is used to find the key for signing. The configuration variable gpg.program
       is used to specify a custom signing binary.

       Tag objects (created with -a, -s, or -u) are called "annotated" tags; they contain a
       creation date, the tagger name and e-mail, a tagging message, and an optional cryptographic
       signature. Whereas a "lightweight" tag is simply a name for an object (usually a commit
       object).

       temporary object labels. For this reason, some git commands for naming objects (like git
       describe) will ignore lightweight tags by default.

We need options: "do not check device numbers when creating" => --no-check-device. "test the archive volume label and exit" => --test-label. So answer: use tar --no-check-device --test-label ... Also maybe combine with -c for create. Provide example command.</think>The two options you need are:

| Purpose | Long option | Short form (if any) |

Both can be used together in a single `tar` invocation.  
A typical command that creates an archive, skips device‑number checking, and then verifies (and exits) the volume label looks like this:

```bash
tar --create \
    --no-check-device \
    --test-label \
    -f archive.tar \
    /path/to/files...
```

* `--create` (`-c`) tells `tar` to create a new archive.  
* `--no-check-device` suppresses the usual device‑number validation that `tar` performs when creating incremental archives.  
* `--test-label` checks the archive’s volume label (the label set with `--label` when the archive was created) and then exits immediately, without proceeding to extraction or listing.  

You can also add other usual options (e.g., `-v` for verbose listing, `-f` to specify the archive file, etc.) as needed.

GIT-REBASE(1)                                Git Manual                               GIT-REBASE(1)

NAME
       git-rebase - Reapply commits on top of another base tip

SYNOPSIS
       git rebase [-i | --interactive] [<options>] [--exec <cmd>]
               [--onto <newbase> | --keep-base] [<upstream> [<branch>]]
       git rebase [-i | --interactive] [<options>] [--exec <cmd>] [--onto <newbase>]
               --root [<branch>]
       git rebase (--continue|--skip|--abort|--quit|--edit-todo|--show-current-patch)

DESCRIPTION
       Transplant a series of commits onto a different starting point. You can also use git rebase
       to reorder or combine commits: see INTERACTIVE MODE below for how to do that.

       For example, imagine that you have been working on the topic branch in this history, and you
       want to "catch up" to the work done on the master branch.

                     A---B---C topic
                    /
               D---E---F---G master

       You want to transplant the commits you made on topic since it diverged from master (i.e. A,
       B, and C), on top of the current master. You can do this by running git rebase master while
       the topic branch is checked out. If you want to rebase topic while on another branch, git
       rebase master topic is a shortcut for git checkout topic && git rebase master.

                             A'--B'--C' topic
                            /
               D---E---F---G master

       If there is a merge conflict during this process, git rebase will stop at the first
       problematic commit and leave conflict markers. If this happens, you can do one of these
       things:

        1. Resolve the conflict. You can use git diff to find the markers (<<<<<<) and make edits
           to resolve the conflict. For each file you edit, you need to tell Git that the conflict
           has been resolved. You can mark the conflict as resolved with git add <filename>. After
           resolving all of the conflicts, you can continue the rebasing process with

               git rebase --continue

        2. Stop the git rebase and return your branch to its original state with

               git rebase --abort

        3. Skip the commit that caused the merge conflict with

               git rebase --skip

       If you don’t specify an <upstream> to rebase onto, the upstream configured in
       branch.<name>.remote and branch.<name>.merge options will be used (see git-config(1) for
       details) and the --fork-point option is assumed. If you are currently not on any branch or
       if the current branch does not have a configured upstream, the rebase will abort.

       Here is a simplified description of what git rebase <upstream> does:

        1. Make a list of all commits on your current branch since it branched off from <upstream>
           that do not have an equivalent commit in <upstream>.

        2. Check out <upstream> with the equivalent of git checkout --detach <upstream>.

        3. Replay the commits, one by one, in order. This is similar to running git cherry-pick
           <commit> for each commit. See REBASING MERGES for how merges are handled.

        4. Update your branch to point to the final commit with the equivalent of git checkout -B

What happens when you run it:

| Step | What Git does |
|------|---------------|
| **1. Interrupts the rebase** | Any in‑progress replay of commits is halted immediately. |
| **2. Resets HEAD** | `HEAD` is moved back to the commit it pointed to before the rebase began (the tip of the branch you were on). |
| **3. Cleans up state** | Any temporary references created during the rebase (e.g., `ORIG_HEAD`, rebase‑merge directories) are removed. |
| **4. Restores the working tree** | The working directory and index are returned to the state they had at the start of the rebase, so any uncommitted changes you had before the rebase are preserved. |
| **5. Leaves the reflog** | The action is recorded in the reflog, so you can always find the pre‑rebase commit with `git reflog` if you ever need to recover it. |

### Typical use case

```bash
# You started a rebase, but something went wrong (e.g., a conflict you can’t resolve)
git rebase --abort
```

Might also mention that it's used to validate the Dockerfile syntax, etc. Provide answer.</think>**`--check` (shorthand for `--call=check`)**

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--check` | Equivalent to `--call=check`. It tells the builder to **only validate / check the Dockerfile and its instructions** without actually building the image. |

### Basic syntax

```bash
docker build --check <path‑or‑url>
```

or, using the long form:

```bash
docker build --call=check <path‑or‑url>
```

### What it does

- Parses the Dockerfile and runs the *check* phase of the build.
- Reports any syntax errors, unsupported instructions, or other issues.
- Does **not** create any containers, run `RUN` commands, or produce an image.
- Exits with a non‑zero status if the check fails.

### Typical use‑case

```bash
# Quickly verify that a Dockerfile has no syntax problems
docker build --check .
```

If the Dockerfile is valid, the command succeeds (exit 0) and prints a short “check successful” message. If there are problems, Docker will list them and exit with a non‑zero code.

### Quick reminder from `docker build --help`

```
--check                         Shorthand for "--call=check"
```

So you can use `--check` on its own; no additional arguments or values are required.

```bash
df -lh --total
```

- Any mount that has essentially no usage (i.e., its usage is “insignificant” compared with the total free space) is omitted.
- A final line **“Total”** appears, summarizing the combined usage of the remaining entries.

The user asked: "What does the --numstat flag do in git diff?" The command output shows that `--numstat` shows numeric diffstat instead of patch. I should explain that. Provide a brief description: it shows number of added and deleted lines per file, plus total, in a format like "added deleted filename". Also mention that it's useful for scripts. Provide example output. I'll answer.</think>`--numstat` tells `git diff` to emit a **numeric diffstat** instead of the usual patch (text) output.

### What it shows
For each file that changed, the line looks like:

```
<added> <deleted> <filename>
```

- **added** – number of lines added in that file.  
- **deleted** – number of lines removed in that file.  
- **filename** – the path of the file.

At the end of the diff you also get a total line:

```
<total_added> <total_deleted> <total_filename> (often just “–” for the name)
```

If a file has only additions or only deletions, the missing side is shown as `0`.

### Typical use‑case
- **Scripting / CI pipelines** – you can easily parse the numbers (e.g., with `awk` or `cut`) to know how many lines were added/removed without dealing with patch formatting.
- Quickly gauge the size of changes without the overhead of full patch text.

### Example

```bash
git diff --numstat HEAD~1 HEAD
```

Sample output:

```
 12  5  src/main.py
  3  0  README.md
 20 15  src/utils.rs
--------------------------------------------------
 35 20  total
```

- `src/main.py`: 12 lines added, 5 lines deleted.  
- `README.md`: 3 lines added, 0 deleted.  
- `src/utils.rs`: 20 added, 15 deleted.  
- The final line is the aggregate total.

### Quick comparison

| Flag | Output format |
|------|----------------|
| `-p` / `--patch` | Human‑readable unified diff (context lines, hunks). |
| `--stat` | Text summary: `5 files changed, 12 insertions(+), 7 deletions(-)`. |
| `--numstat` | Numeric per‑file added/deleted counts (machine‑friendly). |

So, `--numstat` is the go‑to option when you need concise, parseable line‑count information rather than the full diff text.

The user asked: "What does the --privileged flag do in docker exec?" The help output shows: `--privileged           Give extended privileges to the command`. I should explain what that means: it gives the process inside the container extended privileges, essentially similar to running with `--privileged` when starting a container, giving access to all devices, etc. However, note that `docker exec --privileged` may not be as impactful as `docker run --privileged`; the exec flag may not actually do much depending on the container's security settings. I should explain typical behavior: it attempts to give the executed command privileged access, such as access to all devices (e.g., /dev), capability to load kernel modules, etc., but it only works if the container was started with `--privileged` or appropriate capabilities; otherwise it may be ignored.

I'll answer accordingly.</think>The `--privileged` flag for `docker exec` tells Docker to give the command you’re running inside the container **extended privileges**, analogous to what `--privileged` does when you start a container with `docker run`.

### What it actually does
- **Device access**: The command gains access to all devices on the host that are also available inside the container (e.g., `/dev`, `/dev/fuse`, etc.).
- **Capabilities**: It attempts to grant the process inside the container all Linux capabilities (the same set a process has when a container runs with `--privileged`).
- **Security impact**: This effectively makes the executed process almost as powerful as a process running directly on the host (outside any container isolation), so it should only be used when you truly need extra access (e.g., for debugging hardware, loading kernel modules, etc.).

### Practical notes
1. **Container must be privileged** – The flag only has effect if the container itself was started with `--privileged` or with the appropriate capabilities. If the container runs without those permissions, Docker may silently ignore the flag or the command will still be limited by the container’s security profile.
2. **Similar to `docker run --privileged`** – When you run a container with `docker run --privileged`, the whole container gets those rights. Using `--privileged` with `docker exec` only applies to the specific command you exec, not the whole container.
3. **Typical use‑case** – Debugging hardware devices, running tools that need direct access to `/dev` (e.g., GPU tools, device‑mapper, etc.), or performing maintenance that requires extra privileges.

### Example
```bash
docker exec --privileged my-container ls /dev
```
This runs `ls /dev` inside `my-container` with the extra privileges described above.

**Bottom line:** `--privileged` in `docker exec` attempts to give the executed command full access to the host’s devices and capabilities, but its success depends on the container’s own security configuration. Use it cautiously.

```bash
git branch --no-merged -r   # show only remote‑tracking branches that aren’t merged
```

```bash
git branch -v --no-merged
```

And if you prefer a compact one‑liner that also sorts the output, you can use:

```bash
git branch --no-merged --sort=refname
```

We'll answer.</think>The NVIDIA System Management Interface (`nvidia‑smi`) can query the list of processes that are currently using the GPU for compute work.  

The relevant option is **`--query-compute-apps`** (or the short form **`-q`** together with **`--query-compute-apps`**).  

### Typical command

```bash
nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,process_name,command,gpu_utilization,memory_usage --format=csv,noheader
```

**Explanation of the parts**

| Part | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `--query-compute-apps` | Tells `nvidia‑smi` to return the list of active compute processes. |
| `=pid,process_name,command,gpu_utilization,memory_usage` | Specifies which columns you want (you can pick any of the supported properties). |
| `--format=csv,noheader` | Outputs the result as plain CSV without the header line, making it easier to parse or pipe to other tools. |

### Common variations

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| **Show only PID and process name** | `nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,process_name --format=csv,noheader` |
| **Show GPU utilization and memory usage** | `nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=gpu_utilization,memory_usage --format=csv,noheader` |
| **Continuously refresh every second** | `nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps --format=csv,noheader -l 1` |
| **XML output** (useful for scripts) | `nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps --format=xml` |

### What the output looks like

```
12345,python3,python script.py,12%, 512MiB
67890,java,my‑app,23%, 1GiB
...
```

Each row corresponds to a process that is currently occupying the GPU for compute tasks, showing its **PID**, **process name**, **command line**, **GPU utilization** (percentage), and **memory usage** (MiB or GiB).  

You can of course combine `--query-compute-apps` with other query options (e.g., `--query-gpu`) if you need additional GPU‑level information alongside the process list.

GIT-RESET(1)                                 Git Manual                                GIT-RESET(1)

NAME
       git-reset - Set `HEAD` or the index to a known state

SYNOPSIS
       git reset [--soft | --mixed [-N] | --hard | --merge | --keep] [-q] [<commit>]
       git reset [-q] [<tree-ish>] [--] <pathspec>...
       git reset [-q] [--pathspec-from-file=<file> [--pathspec-file-nul]] [<tree-ish>]
       git reset (--patch | -p) [<tree-ish>] [--] [<pathspec>...]

DESCRIPTION
       git reset does either of the following:

        1. git reset [<mode>] <commit> changes which commit HEAD points to. This makes it possible
           to undo various Git operations, for example commit, merge, rebase, and pull.

        2. When you specify files or directories or pass --patch, git reset updates the staged
           version of the specified files.

           git reset [<mode>] [<commit>]
               Set the current branch head (HEAD) to point at <commit>. Depending on <mode>, also
               update the working directory and/or index to match the contents of <commit>.
               <commit> defaults to HEAD. Before the operation, ORIG_HEAD is set to the tip of the
               current branch.

               The <mode> must be one of the following (default --mixed):

               --mixed
                   Leave your working directory unchanged. Update the index to match the new HEAD,
                   so nothing will be staged.

                   If -N is specified, mark removed paths as intent-to-add (see git-add(1)).

               --soft
                   Leave your working tree files and the index unchanged. For example, if you have
                   no staged changes, you can use git reset --soft HEAD~5; git commit to combine
                   the last 5 commits into 1 commit. This works even with changes in the working
                   tree, which are left untouched, but such usage can lead to confusion.

               --hard
                   Overwrite all files and directories with the version from <commit>, and may
                   overwrite untracked files. Tracked files not in <commit> are removed so that the
                   working tree matches <commit>. Update the index to match the new HEAD, so
                   nothing will be staged.

               --merge
                   Reset the index and update the files in the working tree that are different
                   between <commit> and HEAD, but keep those which are different between the index
                   and working tree (i.e. which have changes which have not been added). Mainly
                   exists to reset unmerged index entries, like those left behind by git am -3 or
                   git switch -m in certain situations. If a file that is different between
                   <commit> and the index has unstaged changes, reset is aborted.

               --keep
                   Resets index entries and updates files in the working tree that are different
                   between <commit> and HEAD. If a file that is different between <commit> and HEAD
                   has local changes, reset is aborted.
